title: Forty Days on the Mountain
sum: The book opens on Mount Sinai. In the third month after the Exodus, God calls Moses up to receive the stone tablets, and for forty days in the cloud he shows him "what came first and what is still to come." Before any history is told, God foretells its end: Israel will enter the land, grow full, follow the nations' gods, kill the prophets, lose track of the right days for its feasts, and go into exile.

Moses prays that God will not abandon his people to the spirit of Beliar. God answers with a promise: after they confess their sins, he will circumcise their hearts, give them a holy spirit, and be their father. Then God tells the angel of the presence to write for Moses the whole history from creation until God's sanctuary stands forever on Zion. The angel takes the tablets of the division of the years, and the rest of the book is his dictation.
readings: The chapter tells the reader how to hear everything that follows: as revelation given at Sinai, dated from heavenly tablets and dictated by an angel. The stories of Genesis become part of the law.
Read as prophecy of the writer's own day

The sins listed in 1:8-14, above all the wrong calendar, and the hope of a cleansed people in 1:22-25, fit a Jewish writer of the 100s BC who believed his people had gone astray and were about to be restored.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches read this chapter as Scripture: Moses on Sinai receives both the law and the account of all history, written for him at God's command. The promise of circumcised hearts and a holy spirit is read with the new covenant in Christ.
views.H: Historical critics see a frame written in the 100s BC that borrows the voice of Deuteronomy 31 to say that Israel's history of sin was foreseen, and that the restoration the writer hoped for was promised at Sinai. The stress on the start of the month, the Sabbaths and the jubilees (1:14) shows the book's central quarrel.
views.N: The angel who writes for Moses (1:27) is the earliest clear witness to the belief that the law came through angels, which Acts 7:53, Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2 take for granted. The circumcised heart (1:23) and the children of God (1:24-25) are themes Paul takes up in Romans 2:29 and 2 Corinthians 6:18.
views.J: The Damascus Document from the Dead Sea Scrolls points its readers to a book of the divisions of the times, very likely this one. The rabbis too taught that Moses was shown on Sinai far more than the written Torah.
views.W: Most churches do not read this as Scripture. They value it as evidence of how Jews before Christ read Deuteronomy's warnings and promises, and of the belief in angelic mediation that the New Testament mentions.

echoes: Exodus 19:1; Exodus 24:12-18; Exodus 31:18; Deuteronomy 31:16-29; Deuteronomy 30:1-6; Deuteronomy 9:26-29; Jeremiah 29:13-14; Ezekiel 36:26-27; Psalm 51:10-11; Isaiah 63:9; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2; Romans 2:29; 2 Corinthians 6:15-18; Revelation 21:1-3

settings.why: It names the book and its claim: an account, dated by weeks of years and jubilees, of what the Lord told Moses on Sinai. A reader knows from the first line that the stories of Genesis will be told as revelation with fixed dates.
settings.readers: The book does not name its first readers. The earliest evidence of who read it is the Damascus Document of the Dead Sea Scrolls community, which sends its members to the "Book of Time Divisions by Jubilees and Weeks" (column 16), very likely this book: that group read it and trusted its dates.

settings.what: God foretells Israel's sin, exile and return
settings.when: During the forty days in the cloud, before the tablets are given
settings.why: To have the whole future written down in advance, so that later generations, when disaster comes, will see that God warned them and did not abandon them (1:5-6). The prophecy follows Deuteronomy 31 and turns it into a summary of Israel's history up to the return from exile.
settings.readers: Jews of the Second Temple period who had lived through exile and return and, in the writer's view, still kept the feasts on the wrong days. The list of sins in 1:14 speaks to them directly.
views: Verse 10 describes the fall of the northern kingdom and verses 11-13 the exile of Judah; verse 17 the rebuilding of the Temple.
A prophecy of the writer's own time
Many readers hear in 1:12-14 the struggles of the writer's day, when those who "search out the law" were opposed.

settings.when: After hearing the prophecy of Israel's sin
settings.why: Moses pleads, in words from Deuteronomy 9 and Psalm 51, that God will not hand his people over to the nations or to the spirit of Beliar, and will give them a clean heart. The prayer turns the prophecy of judgment into a request for inner change.
settings.readers: Readers who saw their own people as torn between the nations' ways and God's law heard the prayer as their own.

settings.what: The Lord's promise of a new heart
settings.to: Moses, and through him the angel of the presence (1:27)
settings.why: God promises that after confession he will circumcise their hearts, give a holy spirit, and be their father; then he orders the angel to write the history from creation to the sanctuary on Zion. The promise gives the hearers hope that the story will end in a cleansed Israel and God living among them.
settings.readers: The same Second Temple readers, who looked for that restoration in their own day.

title: Twenty-Two Works and the Sabbath
sum: The angel of the presence begins his dictation with the six days of creation. On the first day God makes the heavens, the earth, the waters, and all the spirits that serve him: the angels of the presence, the angels of holiness, and the angels over fire, wind, cloud and season. One work follows on the second day, four on the third, three on the fourth, three on the fifth and four on the sixth: twenty-two works in all. Only the sun is named as the sign that sets days, months, feasts and jubilees.

Then comes the Sabbath. God gives it first to the two highest ranks of angels, who keep it with him in heaven. He promises to set apart a people from all nations, the descendants of Jacob, his firstborn, to keep it with them on earth. Jacob is the twenty-second head of humankind, as the works were twenty-two. The chapter ends with the Sabbath law: death for work, no cooking, no drawing water, no carrying loads, a day of eating, drinking and blessing for Israel alone.
readings: Most of the chapter follows Genesis 1:1-2:3 closely, filling gaps: when the angels were made, when Eden was planted, how many works there were.
The writer builds the Sabbath and the solar calendar into creation itself, so that keeping them is not one custom among others but the order of the world, shared with the angels.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches read the chapter as Scripture, with Genesis 1: the angels made on the first day, the twenty-two works, and the Sabbath as a holy day blessed at creation.
views.H: Critics see a writer who wanted the Sabbath and the 364-day solar year to rest on creation: hence the sun alone as the sign (2:9) and the Sabbath given to angels before humans. The strict Sabbath rules of 2:29-30 match the hardest positions of Jewish law in the second century BC.
views.N: The chapter shows the Sabbath disputes of the Gospels from the strict side: carrying, preparing food and drawing water forbidden, and death for work (Mark 2:23-3:6; John 5:10). Its angels over the winds and fire are the same figures as in Revelation 7:1 and 14:18.
views.J: The rabbis disagreed on when the angels were made (second or fifth day, by Charles's report of Genesis Rabbah). Midrash Tadshe counts the same twenty-two works and links them to the generations from Adam to Jacob. The rule that Sabbath food must be prepared the day before is shared with later Jewish law.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an early Jewish witness to how Genesis 1 and the Sabbath were understood, not as Scripture. Its claim that the Sabbath is for Israel alone is set beside the New Testament's teaching (Mark 2:27; Colossians 2:16-17).

echoes: Genesis 1:1-2:3; Exodus 31:13-17; Exodus 4:22; Exodus 16:23; Leviticus 20:26; Jeremiah 17:21-22; Nehemiah 13:15-19; Isaiah 58:13; Job 38:7; Psalm 104:4; Revelation 7:1; Revelation 14:18; Mark 2:27; Hebrews 4:9-10

settings.what: The angel's account of the six days
settings.when: On Sinai, at the Lord's command (1:27)
settings.why: To give Moses "the whole account of creation" with its works counted and dated, so that the Sabbath that follows rests on the shape of creation itself.
settings.readers: Readers who argued about the calendar and the Sabbath: the account counts the works so that the Sabbath rests on them, and it makes the sun alone the sign for days, months and feasts (2:9), the year the book defends in 6:23-38 against those who go wrong about it (1:14).

settings.by: The angel of the presence, reporting what God said to the angels (2:19-20)
settings.when: On Sinai, as the conclusion of the creation account
settings.why: The law binds every Israelite, in every home and at every gate, on every seventh day: no work, no cooking, no drawing water, no carrying in or out, and death for whoever breaks it. Its purpose is to keep Israel holy and in the land (2:27), keeping Sabbath with the highest angels. It answers the problem of a people who, in the writer's eyes, treated the Sabbath lightly.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC, for whom keeping the Sabbath had become a mark of loyalty; the book's last chapter returns to the same law (50:6-13).

title: Forty Days, Eighty Days, Seven Years
sum: The angels bring the animals to Adam over five days of the second week, and he names them all. Finding no helper like him, he sleeps, and God builds the woman from his rib. Because Adam was made in the first week and his wife in the second, and because the angels brought Adam into Eden after forty days and the woman after eighty, the law of Leviticus 12 for mothers after a birth is written on the heavenly tablets: forty days for a boy, eighty for a girl. Eden is holy, like the sanctuary.

Adam and Eve work the garden seven years. On the 17th of the second month the snake comes; the woman eats, covers herself, and gives to Adam. God curses the snake, the woman and the ground, clothes them in skins and sends them out. Adam burns incense as he leaves, the animals lose their speech, and a new law is written: Israel must cover its nakedness and not uncover itself as the nations do. Adam and Eve settle in Elda.
readings: The chapter follows Genesis 2:18-3:24 closely, with dates added and the angels doing what God does in Genesis.
Twice the story stops for a law on the heavenly tablets (3:8-14; 3:31). For the writer, Eden explains why Israel keeps the laws of birth purity and modest dress.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches read the chapter as Scripture, with Genesis 2-3 and Leviticus 12: the purity laws and the command to cover nakedness are given their reason in Eden.
views.H: Critics see a writer giving Mosaic laws an origin in Eden. Charles 1902 read 3:31 as a protest against Jews who took part, naked, in the Greek gymnasium in Jerusalem (2 Maccabees 4:9-14), a clue for dating the book.
views.N: The chapter shows the law of purification that Mary keeps in Luke 2:22-24, and a reading of Genesis 2:24 without "the two" that Jesus' quotation has (Matthew 19:5). Adam's incense and Eden's holiness picture Eden as a sanctuary, an image Christian writers also used.
views.J: Charles 1902 notes that Midrash Tadshe gives the same reason for the forty and eighty days, while other rabbis gave Adam only hours in Eden. Josephus agrees that the animals once spoke one language.
views.W: Most churches value the chapter as an early Jewish reading of Genesis 2-3 that explains Leviticus 12 and shows how the Fall was understood before Christ, without reading it as Scripture.

echoes: Genesis 2:18-3:24; Leviticus 12:1-8; Luke 2:22-24; Matthew 19:4-6; Exodus 30:34-38; Exodus 28:42-43; Genesis 11:1; Ezekiel 28:13-14; 2 Maccabees 4:9-14; Revelation 12:9

settings.what: The law of purity after childbirth
settings.by: The angel of the presence, citing the heavenly tablets (3:10)
settings.when: In the story of the creation of Adam and Eve and their entry into Eden
settings.why: The law binds every Israelite mother after a birth: seven days of impurity and thirty-three of purifying for a boy, fourteen and sixty-six for a girl, with no touching holy things and no entering the sanctuary until the days are over. It applies wherever there is a sanctuary to enter. The angel explains why Leviticus 12 has these numbers: they repeat the first week, the second week, and the forty and eighty days before Adam and Eve entered holy Eden.
settings.readers: Israelite mothers, and the priests who ruled on purity, at a time when there was a sanctuary to keep away from (3:13). The angel's hearers are "all who know the judgment of the law" (3:31), that is, Israel.

settings.what: The snake speaks to the woman
settings.when: On the 17th of the second month of the eighth year
settings.why: The dialogue follows Genesis 3:1-5 almost word for word; the date makes the Fall a fixed event in the book's calendar.

settings.what: The curses on the snake, the woman and Adam
settings.to: The snake, the woman and Adam
settings.why: As in Genesis 3:14-19, God's words set the conditions of life outside Eden: pain in childbirth, rule by the husband, a cursed ground and a return to the earth. Jubilees shortens the curse on the snake (see 3:23).

settings.to: Moses, for "all who know the judgment of the law"
settings.when: After God clothes Adam alone of all creatures (3:30)
settings.why: It binds every Israelite, not only the priests at the altar (Exodus 28:42): never to go uncovered as the nations do. It answers a problem the writer saw among his own people.
settings.readers: Charles 1902 read the law as aimed at Jewish young men who exercised naked in the gymnasium built in Jerusalem under Jason (2 Maccabees 4:9-14).

title: Cain, the Watchers and Enoch
sum: Cain, Abel and their sister Awan are born. In the first year of the third jubilee Cain kills Abel; a law against secret murder is written on the heavenly tablets, and the angels say they report every sin to God. Seth is born to replace Abel, and the line runs on through Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel and Jared, each marriage dated and each wife named. In Jared's days the angels of the Lord, the Watchers, come down to teach justice on the earth.

Enoch, Jared's son, is the first to learn writing. He records the signs of the sky and the calendar, sees the future in a dream, testifies against the Watchers who have sinned with women, and is taken into Eden, where he still writes the judgment of the world. The Lord has four holy places: Eden, the Mountain of the East, Sinai and Zion. Adam dies at 930, within the "day" of a thousand years; Cain is killed by the stones of his own falling house; and Noah marries and has three sons.
readings: The chapter keeps the names and the order of Genesis 4-5 and fills every gap: the wives, the dates, how Cain died, where Enoch went.
At its center (4:15-26) stands a summary of the Enoch traditions now in 1 Enoch: the Watchers, the astronomy, the dream visions, Enoch the scribe.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox churches, which also count 1 Enoch as Scripture, read this chapter with it: Enoch is the first writer and the seventh from Adam (Jude 14), taken to God and still testifying.
views.H: Critics see the writer's use of 1 Enoch (the Watchers of 1 Enoch 6-16, the astronomy of 72-82, the dream visions of 83-90) changed to fit his own views: the Watchers are sent down for good and fall later, and Enoch already teaches the jubilee calendar.
views.N: The thousand-year day (4:30) is the same reckoning as 2 Peter 3:8. Enoch taken from death (4:23) stands beside Hebrews 11:5, and the Watchers' sin beside Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4.
views.J: Charles 1902 records later Jewish traditions on Cain's death (a stone or a reed, Genesis Rabbah 22) and on Genesis 4:26 as the start of idolatry. Jewish law, he notes, did not apply 4:32's "same tool" rule.
views.W: Most churches value the chapter as an early witness to the Enoch traditions that Jude and 2 Peter knew, and to Jewish readings of Genesis 4-5, without reading it as Scripture.

echoes: Genesis 4:1-26; Genesis 5:1-32; Genesis 6:1-4; Deuteronomy 27:24; Exodus 21:23-25; Psalm 90:4; 2 Peter 3:8; Hebrews 11:4-5; Hebrews 12:24; Jude 6; Jude 14-15; 1 Enoch 6:6; 1 Enoch 12:4; 1 Enoch 72:1

settings.what: The law against secret murder, and the angels' report
settings.by: The angel of the presence, citing the heavenly tablets
settings.why: The law binds every Israelite: a curse on whoever strikes his neighbor in secret, an "So be it" from the witnesses, and a curse on the witness who keeps silent. The angels add that they report every sin to God. The hearers learn that no hidden crime goes unseen.
settings.readers: Israel, the people who answer "So be it" to the curses of Deuteronomy 27. The law speaks to the witness who keeps quiet as much as to the killer.

settings.why: The angel ties the place where Moses stands, Sinai, to Eden, the Mountain of the East and Zion, and says Zion will make the whole earth holy in the new creation. The hearers learn that their Temple mount belongs to a plan as old as Eden.
settings.readers: Readers who honored Mount Zion and its Temple: the verse says that Zion will make the whole earth holy in the new creation.

settings.what: The law of punishment in kind
settings.by: The angel, citing the heavenly tablets
settings.when: After Cain is killed by stones, as he killed Abel
settings.why: It states the rule of like for like as written in heaven and carried out by God himself. It answers the question why Cain, spared in Genesis 4:15, still died a violent death.
